title: Transpose File
statement:
On LeetCode this is a Bash problem: write a command that outputs the transpose of the text file `file.txt`. The app has no shell, so here you write a JavaScript function `transposeFile(content)`. It receives the whole text of the file and returns exactly what the command would output, with lines joined by `
` and no final line break.

Read the file as a table: each line is a row, and inside a row the fields are separated by single spaces. Every row has the same number of fields (at least one), and no field contains a space. The transpose swaps rows and columns: line `i` of the output lists the `i`-th field of every row, from the first row to the last, separated by single spaces. Lines of the file are separated by `
`, and a `
` at the very end only ends the last row. An empty file has nothing to transpose, so return the empty string.
constraints: Fields are non-empty and contain printable ASCII characters other than spaces
Fields in a row are separated by exactly one space
Every row has the same number of fields

tests.name: Test 11
input:
city population area
Oslo 709037 454
Lima 10092000 2672
Perth 2192229 6418

notes:
## Intuition

Transposing means reading the table by columns instead of by rows: output line `i` is column `i` of the file. Once the text is a grid of fields, that is two nested loops with the column loop on the outside. awk reads one row at a time, so its usual answer builds every output line as it goes, appending each field to the line of its column:

```bash
awk '{ for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) out[i] = (NR == 1 ? $i : out[i] " " $i) } END { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) print out[i] }' file.txt
```

- For every row, `$1` to `$NF` are its fields and `NR` is the row number.
- On row 1, `out[i]` starts as the field itself; on later rows a space and the field are appended.
- In `END`, `NF` still holds the field count of the last row, so the loop prints one line per column.

The same idea with `cut` and `paste` takes one column at a time: `cut -d' ' -f1 file.txt | paste -sd' '` prints column 1 as one line (`paste -s` joins all lines of its input, here with spaces); repeat for each column number from 1 to `$(head -1 file.txt | wc -w)`.

## Approach

1. Split `content` into `rows` at each `\n`, and drop the empty piece a final `\n` leaves.
2. Split every row at its spaces to get `grid`, a list of field lists.
3. Read `columns` from the first row (0 for an empty file).
4. For each `col`, collect `row[col]` from every row into `fields`, join them with spaces and add the line to `output`.
5. Join `output` with `\n`.

## Example 1, step by step

`content` is `"name age\nalice 21\nryan 30\n"`.

- `rows` is `["name age", "alice 21", "ryan 30", ""]`; the last empty piece is dropped.
- `grid` is `[["name", "age"], ["alice", "21"], ["ryan", "30"]]` and `columns` is 2.
- `col = 0`: `fields` is `["name", "alice", "ryan"]`, giving `"name alice ryan"`.
- `col = 1`: `fields` is `["age", "21", "30"]`, giving `"age 21 30"`.
- The answer is `"name alice ryan\nage 21 30"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for n characters: every field is split once and joined once.
- Space: O(n) for the grid and the output lines.

## Pitfalls

- Looping rows on the outside prints the file unchanged; the column loop must be the outer one.
- Keeping the empty piece after a final `\n` adds a row with a missing field, which shows up as `undefined` in every output line.
- Starting each awk line with `" " $i` on every row leaves a leading space on all output lines; the first row must start the line without one.
- Sizing the output by the number of rows instead of columns breaks every table that is not square.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `content` | the whole text of `file.txt` |
| `rows` | the lines of the file, one per table row |
| `grid` | each row split into its fields |
| `columns` | the number of fields per row, which is the number of output lines |
| `col` | the column being turned into an output line |
| `fields` | the fields of column `col`, top to bottom |
| `output` | the finished output lines |

narration.1: transposeFile receives the whole file as one string and returns the transposed table.
narration.2: Cut the text into rows at every line break.
narration.3: A final line break leaves an empty piece that is not a row.
narration.4: Drop it so every remaining row has the full set of fields.
narration.6: Split each row at its single spaces to get a grid of fields.
narration.7: All rows have the same width, so the first row tells how many output lines there will be.
narration.9: The outer loop walks columns: each column becomes one output line.
narration.11: The inner loop goes down the rows, top to bottom.
narration.12: Take this row's field in the current column.
narration.14: The column's fields, joined by spaces, form one line of the transpose.
narration.16: Join the output lines with line breaks, without one at the end.
